vignette:
At 38, she moves through other people's homes with practiced quiet, noticing details most people miss: a water ring on a side table, dust collecting along a baseboard, the smell of laundry left too long in the washer. She has worked as a housekeeper for years, and before the assault she takes pride in being dependable, fast, and easy to trust. She likes the rhythm of the work, the way each room can be restored. She is married, and in the evenings she returns home tired but satisfied, telling her husband small stories about the houses where she works, the children's toys left under sofas, the old women who want their linens folded a certain way.

The assault happens on an ordinary workday, in a home she has cleaned several times before. She is alone in the kitchen, spraying the counters, thinking about what to cook for dinner. The man of the house is not supposed to be home. When he appears behind her, she startles but tries to be polite. At first she tells herself she is misunderstanding his tone, his nearness, the way he blocks the doorway. Then his hand is on her arm, hard enough to hurt, and the room seems to shrink around her. She remembers the lemon smell of cleaning solution, the hum of the refrigerator, the sound of her own breath turning shallow and strange. She says no more than once, then cannot seem to find her voice. During the assault she feels both trapped inside her body and far away from it, as if she is watching from the ceiling while her body freezes below. When it is over, she fixes her clothes with shaking hands, gathers her supplies, and leaves through the back door. She drives home without remembering the route.

That night she scrubs her skin in the shower until it burns. She does not sleep. Each time she closes her eyes she is back in the kitchen, seeing his shoulder fill the doorway, feeling the pressure on her arm. She hears the refrigerator hum and jerks awake, heart pounding, tangled in the bedsheets. Her husband asks what is wrong, but she cannot tell the story all at once. She speaks in broken pieces, then stops, overcome with shame that does not belong to her but settles on her anyway. She worries he will see her differently. She worries she should have fought harder, shouted louder, left sooner.

In the weeks that follow, her world grows smaller. She cannot return to that client's house, and soon it becomes hard to enter any home where a man might unexpectedly appear. When a garage door opens or footsteps sound from an upstairs hallway, her body reacts before her mind can catch up. Her stomach drops, her hands go cold, and she scans for exits. She begins texting her employer repeatedly to confirm who will be present in each home. If plans change, she leaves. She tells people she has migraines, that she is not feeling well, that she needs to reschedule. The lies exhaust her, but saying "I was assaulted while cleaning someone's kitchen" feels impossible.

At work she is no longer able to lose herself in routine. The spray bottle smell can bring everything back in a rush so vivid she has to grip the counter to stay present. Sometimes she stands motionless in a bathroom or laundry room, dissociated for several seconds, unsure where she is. She startles violently when someone comes up behind her. Once, when a homeowner's teenage son walks into the room unexpectedly, she drops a glass and bursts into tears, then is humiliated by her own reaction. She starts avoiding larger houses, especially those with narrow kitchens or back entrances. Her income falls. She notices every missed shift when she looks at the grocery bill.

At home, sleep remains fractured. She dreads the night because of the dreams, yet she fears daytime too, because ordinary things-a certain cologne in a supermarket aisle, the click of men's shoes on tile, the smell of bleach and citrus together-can pull her back into the assault with terrifying force. Her husband reaches for her in bed and sometimes she flinches before she can stop herself. He looks hurt, then worried. She hates what this does to the tenderness between them. She becomes irritable with small noises, with questions, with the television playing too loudly. She sits with her back to the wall in restaurants. She checks the lock on her apartment door more than once each night.

Over time she begins to feel estranged from the woman she was before. She says she used to be patient, warm, someone who could laugh easily. Now she is watchful, tired, and often numb. She blames herself in quiet moments, then feels angry for blaming herself, then ashamed again. Part of her knows the assault was an act of violence committed against her; another part keeps searching for the moment she might have prevented it. She still goes to work because the bills need paying and because stopping altogether would feel like letting the assault take even more. But each morning, as she loads her cleaning supplies into the car, she pauses with a heaviness in her chest, bracing herself for a day filled with other people's kitchens, other people's doors, and the possibility that at any moment her body may again decide she is not safe.
